title: AI demand is still running ahead of supply, but the compute bottleneck is turning into a political problem
dek: Glen Kacher of Light Street sees AI as a 15-to-20-year rebuild of the computing stack, and only a third of the way through the first phase; the real risk is not over-investment in CapEx but power and local politics slowing construction.
why: A tech hedge fund investor at the center of Silicon Valley connects AI compute, semiconductors, open-source models and the power bottleneck into one investable chain of reasoning, at high information density.
who: Investors watching AI compute, semiconductors and tech stocks, and founders who want to understand data center power and local political risk.
skip: The opening 0:00-14:35, covering his resume and lineage, can be fast-forwarded; low information density.

points.h: Buy only the best company, never the second or third
points.body: Over 13 years at Integral Capital, Kacher made 46 private investments, and the lesson he drew is: do not buy the second- or third-best company in an industry, always buy the best one you can get. The reason is that in tech the leader takes two-thirds of the market, the number two gets 20% to 25% at most, and everyone else fights over scraps. Higher margins plus a dominant share compound the lead. But he also concedes that incumbents in tech get disrupted, and disruption usually comes not from big companies but from small ones — AI and the semiconductors behind AI are exactly the test case for that rule.

Kacher says many people assume Nvidia will lose its roughly 85% share of the AI accelerator market, and the shift to inference does give competitors an opening. But he thinks the market currently underestimates Nvidia's own capacity to innovate. He describes the evolution of inference chips as an alphabet progression from CPU to FPU to GPU to XPU, where X stands for the unknown: Google has TPU, there are other approaches like Trainium, and Nvidia itself acquired the Grok inference line. He judges that inference will ultimately be a bigger market than training, so there will be many chip form factors and many opportunities to innovate.

points.h: Four semiconductor companies are 40% of the portfolio
points.body: TSMC, Nvidia, Broadcom and AMD make up roughly 40% of Light Street's public holdings, a highly concentrated portfolio. Kacher's logic: concentrate capital where innovation is densest, and right now the densest place is the core of AI accelerated computing. Nvidia has more than 80% of the GPU networking market, and AMD is catching up; as agentic AI becomes the next growth driver, AMD has a unique advantage because it is one of the two big players in both desktop and server CPUs; Broadcom has built TPUs for Google for years and now has opportunities with big players like OpenAI; TSMC fabricates for all three, so it wins no matter who wins, an almost oligopolistic or even monopolistic position.

points.h: Open-source models are fighting a price war
points.body: Kacher thinks the battle between Anthropic and OpenAI is happening in real time, and that Google remains a player thanks to Gemini and its search distribution advantage, so it cannot be ruled out. But the battlefield that is really emerging is open-source models: they are free, can be downloaded to run on local hardware, or run on someone else's commoditized hardware in the cloud, competing directly with the two big companies' expensive frontier models. He judges that early signals show both approaches have their place. At the same time he points to the regulatory problem: open-source models can be put into your own software and tuned to your needs, and regulators actually have few options, because these models are already out in the wild.

points.h: Someone was already saying GPUs should do AI in 2005
points.body: Kacher recalls that at Integral, Kleiner Perkins partner Bill Joy mentioned a group of engineers at Caltech using GPUs for early AI computation, around 2005 or 2006, and Bill Joy's conclusion was that the GPU would be the chip architecture best suited to AI computation. It stayed in his head. Later, on every visit to Nvidia, Jensen would talk about AI, but at the time AI was only a tiny end market for Nvidia, and crypto mattered far more. In the second half of 2022 the crypto crash and the takeoff of AI happened at the same time, the market was more focused on crypto and pushed the stock down, which in turn gave them the chance to build a position in Nvidia.

points.h: The giants are not over-investing, they are catching up
points.body: Faced with the challenge that AI could be over-provisioned like fiber, Kacher's answer is: Amazon, Microsoft and Google are building the compute stack in partnership with Anthropic and OpenAI, and the question is how far ahead of demand they are planning. His judgment is that today they are not ahead, they are behind and catching up. The bears expect them to over-invest, but that is not happening today. He concedes there are real bottlenecks, including the memory companies and TSMC, which cannot invest as fast as they would like, so today demand is still running far ahead of supply, and the pessimism around AI is misplaced.

points.h: A fifteen-year cycle, and only a third of it is done
points.body: Kacher likens AI to the shift from client-server to internet architecture, a computing cycle that happens roughly every 15 to 25 years. The old technology was a search-and-retrieve model, with data stored in databases; AI generates a custom answer for your question and your data on every use, and is far more compute-intensive. The rhythm he gives: infrastructure development takes about 5 to 10 years, years 6 to 16 are when the platform or operating system takes shape, and years 11 to 21 are when applications become the main venue for enterprise investment and innovation. By that framework, roughly a third of the first phase is done, and the whole cycle is at least 15 to 20 years.

points.h: Power and local politics have become the new bottleneck
points.body: Kacher treats political resistance to data centers as a real risk: any bottleneck that slows technology adoption is a problem. He says it is not yet a big problem today, but it is an emerging one. His solution is that the industry has to explain itself proactively: Northern Virginia, as the data center capital of the world, has brought the area tax revenue and blue-collar demand for electricians, plumbers and construction workers, a shot in the arm for the economy. He mentions a data center project in San Mateo that plans to put Bloom Energy natural gas fuel cells behind the meter, with almost no emissions and almost no noise, and residents still opposed it because they had heard data centers are bad. He sees this as an education problem, requiring project-by-project explanation of energy, jobs and tax revenue, from local to national.
